latin: Materia nullum dicit actum entitatiuum positiuum.
translation: Matter signifies no positive entitative act.
translation_note: 'actus entitativus' recurs as Pico's own term for an act constitutive of a thing's positive being (cf. thesis 2.34); matter, on this thesis, contributes none (farmer1998:11767).
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch4, from Latin at farmer1998:11767

sources.text: Thomas Aquinas, Scriptum super libros Sententiarum, 2, d. 18, q. 1, a. 2
sources.pico_relation: Edelheit's identified locus for Thomas's account of divine action on matter through seminal reasons, behind the thesis's denial that matter is a positive act

doctrine: The thesis denies that matter, considered in itself, constitutes any positive actuality; Farmer notes the underlying question was whether the matter of created beings belongs to their formal essence or definition, on which Pico here follows the negative side, cross-referenced to theses 7.21, 8.6, 18.3 and 2>52 (farmer1998:11807). Edelheit reports that Thomas, commenting on the Sentences (2, d.18, q.1, a.2), discusses how God operates on matter through seminal reasons and concludes that matter is purely [potential] (edelheit2022:12267).
historiography: Edelheit (2022) connects thesis 33 to Thomas's Sentences commentary on divine action on matter through seminal reasons (edelheit2022:12267); Farmer (1998) situates it within a cluster of cross-referenced theses on whether matter enters into the definition of natural substances (farmer1998:11807).

quotations.text: impossibile est aliquid idem affirmare et negare; sed si in aliquo distinguantur affirmationes et negationes pertinentes ad illam distinctionem, de ipso verificari poterunt: quia omnis distinctio, sive rei sive rationis, fundatur in affirmatione et negatione

not_established: The completion of Thomas's argument that matter is 'purely [...]' is cut off in the material consulted; its exact wording is not established from the sources at hand (edelheit2022:12267).
